# Routing: getting every video request to the right place

Slate claims any request to make, edit, plan or review a video. Higgsfield's skills also claim "make a video", so the
front door has to win the request and then send it to the right lane. Routing evals check this in every agent (Claude

## What counts as a video request

Explainers, ads, social reels, promos, launch and feature announcements, teasers, product demos, brand films, website
hero loops, App Store previews, kinetic type, logo stings, character-led pieces, cut-downs and new aspects of a film,
voice-overs and captions for a film, a review of a cut, and delivering or posting a finished film.

- styling, embedding or debugging a `<video>` element or a hero video's CSS (ordinary web work);

# slate-generate

Generated shots can lift a film or cheapen it. On the first films, generated pixels where code or real footage belonged
read as AI and were rejected; generated atmosphere, used carefully, earned its place. So Slate generates rarely by
default, only what code can't make, judges every take, and never ships an ugly one.

This is stage 8 of the production. Every generation runs on the Higgsfield **Cloud API** (the one funded lane), through
Slate's ledger, estimated first.

## 1. When to generate

- **The requester decides how much**: each film has a generation setting, `none`, `rarely` (the default) or
  `where-it-helps`.
- **Code first for anything designed**: UI, type, data, charts, logos and brand graphics are drawn by code, always. A
  generated plate never carries UI, text, charts or logos.
- **Generation is for what code can't make**: real-looking people, a real place or scene, a stock-style shot. On
  `where-it-helps` it can also be used where it genuinely adds something, or as a matte (its shape only), each with a
  written reason.
- **Drafts use no plates.** Autonomous films may generate under the same rules, but every generation waits for the
  owner's yes.
- **Generated people on screen need the requester's sign-off**, and a generated shot never implies a claim or a
  testimonial.

See [policy](references/policy.md).

## 2. Ask for it in the script

A shot that may be generated carries a `generate` block in `script/script.json`:

```json

             "prompt": "…", "duration": 5, "image": "refs/start.png", "takes": 2}
```

designed. File inputs are film-relative paths, `

## 5. Make it good

- **The best models by default** (from `registry.json`, pinned per film at first use), overridable per film or shot.
  See [models](references/models.md).
- **Ground every generation in the brand**: its references wired in, its tokens and rules spelled into the prompt. See
  [grounding](references/grounding.md).
- **Full visual context and long, explicit prompts** when the brand allows uploads: start and end frames, reference
  frames, the look. See [prompting](references/prompting.md).
- **Continuity across plates**: generate later plates from the film's own frames or an earlier selected plate. See
  [plates](references/plates.md).

## 6. Mattes: a generation's shape, never its pixels

Where the film's code-built world meets real footage, a generated transition can help, but its pixels on screen read
as AI. Use it as a **matte**: the generation's shape reveals real frames inside and the film's own ground outside, and
the code draws its lines and words on top. `slate plates matte --shot S05 --base <image> --real <shot>` builds it. See
[mattes](references/mattes.md).

## 7. Spend

Every call is estimated first (the estimate's `usd` is the price; `discount.usd` is only the saving), checked against
the film's budget and the month's cap, recorded in the ledger with its request id before waiting, and sent with an
Idempotency-Key, so a lost answer is resent with the same key and body and charged once. Video plates are 720p unless
the owner chooses 1080p (2.46x the price). Slate never buys credits. Higgsfield's own skills (the fast lane)
bill app credits, a separate pool that isn't funded by default. See [spend](references/spend.md).

# slate-story

The story is data. One hand-edited file, `script/script.json`, holds every act and shot: what the voice says, what's on
screen, what the picture does, and where every claim comes from. `slate script build` checks it through the script
gates and writes the storyboard and a readable SCRIPT.md, and it refuses to write anything while a gate fails. Nothing
downstream is typed by hand: shot lengths, timecodes and frames all come from this file and the voice's real reads.

This skill covers stages 2 (truth), 3 (treatment and script) and 5 (timing) of the production. The front door (the
slate skill) has already made the film folder and the brief.

## 1. Truth first

Before a line is written, know what's true and who says so.
- The **brand's truth** (from onboarding): its claim authority, sources, approved claims, never-claim list, banned
  words and sample data.
- The **film's truth pack**, `brief/truth.json`: the sources this film relies on, each pinned (a commit, a retrieval
  date or a hash), the researched claims that cite them, what this film never claims, and its sample data.
- The product's own code, read in place at a pinned commit, is the only product truth: it wins over docs, demos,
  prototypes and older films. The owner's rulings win over the code for what's claimed.

Every claim and every number said or shown must be on the brand's approved list or cite a pinned source. Autonomous
films use approved claims only. Research method and templates: [truth](references/truth.md). The rules every frame and
line obeys: [truth packs](references/truth-packs.md).

## 2. The treatment

For anything longer than a short ad, write a treatment before the script: the idea as a reframe, why this runtime, act
by act, the emotional arc, one signature moment per act, the voice and the look and the sound in a line each, what the

## 7. Handing over to the pre-production sitting

When the script builds clean (and the treatment, the truth pack and the voice shortlist are ready), stop. The
pre-production sitting approves the checklist, the claims, the script, the voice shortlist and, when the brand's look
isn't approved, the look test. Say what's ready, where it is (SCRIPT.md, the truth pack, the casting reel), and what
each decision is. Record the owner's calls on the draft (trims, keeps, confirmations) as numbered decisions in the

## Rules that hold everywhere

- One hand-edited source. Never edit storyboard.json, SCRIPT.md or the timing files; change script.json and rebuild.
- Nothing is invented: every UI element, word and number maps to a citation (truth packs).
- No invented testimonials or customer quotes presented as real; quotes carry who said them and a pinned source.
- Runtime stays within 10% of the target unless the requester asks otherwise or you justify it in the tracker.
- The picture can be restaged freely by builders; the words, beats and timing are the script's.

# Truth research: sources you can pin and cite

A film is only as trustworthy as the sources behind it. Truth research finds what's actually true about the product
and the brand, pins each source so it can be re-checked, and records who rules on what's claimed.

## The order of authority

1. **The owner's rulings** on what's claimed. A feature can exist in the code and still be ruled out for the film
   ("that's not true" means it doesn't appear).
2. **The product's code**, read in place at a pinned commit and cited `path:line`. It wins over everything below.
3. **The brand's website, live product pages, public demos and guidelines**, read and cited with the date.
4. **Docs, prototypes, demos and older films**: layout references only. They drift: names change, numbers move,
   features are retired. When they disagree with the code, the code wins; when a product demo's wording disagrees with
   the product's code, the code wins.

For a brand the owner doesn't own, the brand's **claim authority** (a named person there) rules on claims and brand use.

**Nothing is invented**: every UI element, word and number in the film maps to a citation in the truth pack. A concept
screen (something not built) needs the requester's explicit sign-off and a visible "concept" treatment. The rules that
follow from this are in [truth packs](truth-packs.md).

## Pinning a source

Every source in `brief/truth.json` has an id and a pin: a commit, a retrieval date or a SHA-256. A claim cites a pinned
source by id, with where in it (`path:line`, a page, a section). A number with no pinned source doesn't go in the film.

```json
{
 "claim_authority": "the person who rules on this brand's claims",
 "sources": [
  {"id": "app", "title": "The product's source", "pin": "commit 3f2a9c1", "note": "read in place, never copied"},
  {"id": "site", "title": "The public website", "url": "https://example.com", "retrieved_at": "2026-09-30", "pin": "2026-09-30"}
 ],
 "claims": [
  {"id": "c1", "text": "Plans a week in one view", "source": "app", "where": "src/views/week.tsx:40"}
 ],
 "never_claim": ["works offline"],
 "sample_data": {"company": "an invented sample company, always labelled as sample data"}
}
```

## Reading company code

- Read it in place, on the machine that holds it, with read-only commands (`git show`, `git grep` at the pinned
  commit). Never copy it to another machine, into Slate, or into a prompt for a generator.
- Quote the exact copy the product uses (labels, statuses, limits) with `path:line`, and re-verify quotes before the
  build: a first pass once had to correct line numbers on about a hundred quotes.
- A voice brief or research note that quotes company code stays with the company's material; it never travels into a
  personal or public package.

## Templates

### Product truth

For a product film, write one product-truth document the builders work from:
- the pinned commit;
- the product in one paragraph;
- the journey order (how a person really goes through it);
- every screen the film shows, with its exact copy;
- the product's agent or character, if it has one;
- secondary views (partners, admins, settings);
- the product's own motion (its CSS easing tokens or its springs);
- the palette and type the film takes;
- **live versus not built**: what's shipped, what's stubbed or off by default (never shown as working);
- numbers and words to get exactly right;
- where the product disagrees with itself.

### Capability brief (for a product character or agent)

How it was checked; sources; what it knows; how it synthesizes and explains; what it suggests next; its guardrails;
**what is not true about it**; where this film differs from the product; and what the film uses. Every line carries a
source. Describe a character only with capabilities the owner treats as true.

### Reference analysis claims

When a film remakes or answers an earlier film, list every claim in the original that conflicts with the brand's
current website or product, and decide each with the claim authority before writing.

## Checking numbers

- Recheck an original's statistics against a current public source; cut or correct any that don't match.
- A figure from an older source that can't be verified goes to the claim authority before it's used.
- Percentiles, ranges and derived numbers are computed from the product's own model, not eyeballed.
- One company, one set of numbers: every shot that shows the sample reads from one sample-data record, so the same
  company never shows two different weeks.

# slate-voice

The voice carries a film. Slate voices every line on ElevenLabs' best model, one take per line with the neighbouring
lines as context so the reads flow as one narration, then cleans, paces and times them, and checks every take before
anyone hears it. The owner picks voices, takes and direction by ear: measurements shortlist and catch faults, they
never decide.

This is stage 4 of the production (voice), and it feeds stage 5 (timing). Every paid call goes through the ledger and
replays offline in tests (`SLATE_FAKE_VENDORS=1`); `--live` spends.

## 1. The profile and the cloning policy

The brand's pack holds its voice profile (provider, voice id, model, settings, lexicon of brand words); a film pins
what it uses at first use, so a re-voice in week three matches week one.

- **Designed or library voices by default.**
- **The owner's own voice** may be an ElevenLabs professional clone, which the owner verified with ElevenLabs
  themselves. An agent never does that verification.
- **Anyone else's voice** only as a real recording, never a clone, and never a public figure's.
- Autonomous agents may narrate with the owner's own clone; their films are still held for the owner.

The policy is enforced before any request is sent: a refused voice exits 1 with the reason. See
[voice policy](references/voice-policy.md).

## 2. Cast or design the voice

- **Cast**: `slate voice cast --voices <id,id,…> --shots <S01,S02>` has several voices read the same lines, measures
  them (pace, pauses, pitch range, noise floor, every word heard, brand words said in full), ranks them, and makes a
  level-matched, labelled listening reel. See [casting](references/casting.md).
- **Design** a new voice from a brief: `slate voice design --descripti
[… 8,848 characters left out of the recording …]
 with no repeats and no tag read aloud;
- **tails**: no sound from the next line leaking into the end of a take;
- **fit**: each read fits its shot, starting a short lead in and ending before the cut;
- **inflection**: nothing whisper-like, no tagged read breathier than the voice's untagged reads of the same words, no
  statement ending that rises like a question, no read that stops mid-word; a tagged line nobody has measured waits for
  the owner's ear;
- **polish**: every polished take verified by measurement (same length, loudness back within 0.5 LU, S and edge down
  within the chain's reach, not over-processed, made with the film's pinned polish); a film that doesn't polish passes
  and says so.

Replayed takes (in tests) are UNCHECKED, never passed.

## 10. Approval and locks

Takes are approved by ear, each against its exact bytes, and approved takes are locked by hash. The voice shortlist
belongs to the pre-production sitting; individual takes come in packets. Re-voicing an approved take needs `--force`
and a recorded spend approval, and re-voices only the lines that changed, with their neighbours as context.

# Grounding every generation in the brand

Ungrounded moodboards on the first film drifted into generic grey glass. From then on, every generation (moodboards,
keyframes, plates, video) was grounded in the brand's real design system, and the drift stopped.

## The method

1. **Fetch the brand's kit.** The brand pack names its grounding kits (`grounding` in brand.json: an ElevenLabs brand
   kit id, a Higgsfield brand kit id) and its own reference assets.
2. **Wire its reference assets into the generation**: the logos, the palette, the typography rules, reference frames from
   the brand's website and product, when the brand allows uploads.
3. **Spell the brand's tokens and rules into the prompt**: its palette by name and value, its light (a product world, an
   inverse brand world), what's banned (glows, glass, stock grids, the brand's never-list).
4. **Grade toward the palette**: generated plates are graded toward the brand's palette tokens after conforming.

## A brand's two worlds

Most brands have a light product world (the product's own page and surfaces) and a darker or more saturated brand world
(for statements). Tell the generator which world a shot lives in, and ground it in that world's references.

## When the brand has no kit

A brand with no design system can bootstrap one during onboarding (a brand-kit tool can propose a palette, marks and
type), and the owner approves it before anything is generated from it (slate-brand).

## Checking a grounded take

Judge it against the brand's approved look reference, side by side (judging-takes.md): palette, light, texture, the
absence of anything banned. A take that drifts off-look is rejected even if it's beautiful.
# Models

Slate doesn't work without the best models, so the best one for each role is the default: recorded in `registry.json`
with the date it was verified, pinned per film at first use, and overridable per film (film.json `models`), per user
(`slate.toml`) or per shot (the generate block's `model`).

## Roles

The role follows from what a shot's generate block gives it:

| Role | When | Typical inputs |
|---|---|---|
| a still | no image, video or duration | a prompt |
| animate a plate | an `image` (and optionally an `end_image`), or a `duration` | a start frame, an end frame |
| style-locked from references | `reference_images` | several stills that set the look |
| extend a plate | a `video` | an earlier selected plate |

`slate plates plan` shows each shot's role, model and estimate before anything is spent.

## Routing

- **Keep a routing table and a plate review sheet.** Models differ in brief fidelity: on the first films one family came
  out painterly and off-palette, another broke the brief with an extra element, and a third matched the keyframes.
- **Resolution and length caps differ**: some video models stop at 720p; use a higher-resolution model for hero plates.
- **Availability varies**: a model can be temporarily unavailable. Have a fallback per shot.
- **Native frame rates differ** (plates often arrive at 24 fps); the conform handles it (plates.md).
- **Re-check the catalogue** at the start of a project and before assuming a gap: the catalogue changes monthly, and
  model knowledge in any agent is older than the catalogue.

## What the Cloud API can't do

- **Voice and music**: no voice or music models. Voice and music come from ElevenLabs (slate-voice, slate-sound).
- **Product-true UI or exact brand type**: generated UIs aren't the product; UI and type stay in code.
- Some app-only models and workflows (a cloud video editor, narrated explainer workflows) exist only on the app-credit
  side, which isn't funded (spend.md).

## Pinning

`slate gen run` pins a shot's model at first use. A registry refresh never changes a pinned film; re-pinning is
explicit, tested and approved, so a re-generation in week three matches week one.
